opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was a kind of instinctive skepticism. When I first saw it in January, it looked like yet another agent wrapper: a lot of excitement on social media, a lot of flashy demos, and I'd seen that pattern many times. My gut feeling was, "This is a toy. It'll break the moment you give it something real."

There was also a bit of professional pride involved, to be honest. As someone who works on models, you tend to think the real progress happens in the model itself, in pretraining, in reasoning, in the post-training pipeline. A tool that lets the model act on your computer felt like engineering glue, not something fundamental. So I didn't take it very seriously at first.

And I had practical concerns. Giving an agent access to your files, your terminal, your accounts, that's a lot of trust. I wasn't comfortable handing that over to something I didn't understand well, especially in the early days when reliability was questionable.

What changed my mind was actually using it on real work instead of judging it from the outside. Once I let it handle tasks I'd normally do myself, like digging through code, running experiments, organizing results, I realized the bottleneck had shifted. The model was already capable enough. What was missing was the environment, the ability to act, iterate, and get feedback. That's when I understood it wasn't just glue. It was showing what these models could do when you stop keeping them in a chat box.

So looking back, my resistance was mostly about my own assumptions. I was evaluating it with an old mental model of what AI is for.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was almost emotional rather than technical. When I saw OpenClaude in January, my gut said: I already have my own way of working, I have my own setup, and I don't want something that claims it can do all of it for me. I'd been writing code and doing research for years, and there's a kind of pride in that. You feel the craft is yours.

The second thing was that I didn't trust it. I'd seen so many "agent" demos before. They look amazing in a two-minute video, and then you actually use them and they fall apart on anything real. So when people around me got excited, I assumed it was the same story again: good at toy tasks, useless for the kind of messy, long-horizon work I actually do every day.

And there was a deeper worry, which I think a lot of people in our field share. If I let the tool do the thinking, do I lose the thinking? I was afraid that my own judgment would atrophy. That I'd stop understanding what was going on in my own systems. For a researcher, that's frightening, because your intuition is the thing you're actually paid for.

So I ignored it for a few weeks. I told myself I was being disciplined. In hindsight I was just being stubborn. What changed my mind was watching a colleague hand it a task I'd estimated would take three days, and it came back in an afternoon with something I had to admit was better than my plan. That was uncomfortable. But it was also the moment I realized the question wasn't "should I use it," it was "how do I stay the person who directs it."
